result: The authors developed a mathematical model based on multitype branching processes to predict resistance dynamics in solid tumors, building on previous work that successfully predicted resistance in colorectal cancer. The model makes simplifying assumptions including constant birth/death rates and neglects spatial/metabolic constraints.
status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly requested clarification on how the new model differs from previous models and how it handles solid tumors (point 1). They also asked for discussion of limitations regarding spatial structure and non-homogeneous growth rates, indicating concern about the branching process model's ability to handle these complexities. This suggests reviewers found the methodological approach needed better justification.

result: The authors parameterized their model using clinical data from 68 melanoma lesions in 20 patients treated with vemurafenib, calculating growth rates (0.01/day), cell division time (7 days), birth rate (0.14/day), and treatment-induced decline rates (-0.03/day median).
status_reasoning: Reviewers raised two significant concerns about these parameters. Point 3 questions whether results from BRAF mutant melanoma can be extrapolated to all cancers. Point 5 challenges the 7-day cell doubling assumption based on a single reference, noting this is difficult to measure and asking how predictions would change if this were different. These concerns indicate uncertainty about parameter validity and generalizability.

result: The model predicts that dual therapy results in long-term disease control for most patients only if there are no cross-resistance mutations. With even one cross-resistance mutation possible, dual therapy has minimal chance of curing patients. In the 22-patient cohort, 8 patients with smallest tumor burden would have >95% cure probability without cross-resistance, but none would be cured with one cross-resistance mutation.
status_reasoning: Reviewers found the paper to be 'an important contribution based on elegant modeling work' and did not challenge these core findings. The editorial decision was favorable, and no reviewer questioned the validity of these predictions about dual therapy outcomes under different cross-resistance scenarios.

result: The model demonstrates that simultaneous therapy with two drugs is much more effective than sequential therapy. Sequential therapy always fails even without cross-resistance mutations, while simultaneous therapy offers 26.3% cure rate with one cross-resistance mutation and 99.9% success without cross-resistance.
status_reasoning: Reviewers did not challenge these findings comparing simultaneous versus sequential therapy. One reviewer specifically suggested moving supplementary figure 3 into the main text (point 2), stating this would 'greatly enhance the impact of the paper by making the result immediately and intuitively clear,' indicating strong support for this result.

result: The model predicts that in patients with large disease burden, triple therapy is needed, but therapy with three agents will not cure patients if there is even one mutation conferring cross-resistance to all three agents.
status_reasoning: Reviewers did not question these predictions about triple therapy. The overall favorable evaluation and lack of specific critique of these claims suggests acceptance of the findings regarding the need for triple therapy and its limitations with cross-resistance.

result: The authors discuss cancer stem cells, noting that in CML they represent only 0.1% of cells, while in solid tumors the fraction is usually >5% and sometimes close to 100%. The model predicts combination treatments will be more effective in cancers with small fractions of tumor stem cells.
status_reasoning: Reviewers specifically raised concern about this topic in point 6, stating 'the probability of cure with one or two drugs is greatly increased in tumors where the only cells that contribute to relapse are rare cancer stem cells. This is a logical and important distinction but seems to be quickly dismissed as not relevant clinically.' Reviewers noted 'Since the cancer stem cell question remains murky, this deserves more comment,' indicating the treatment of this issue was insufficient.

result: The authors acknowledge their results are not readily applicable to immunotherapies (CTLA-4, PD1, CD19-CARs) because the immune system can replicate and evolve, and long-term disease control is more common with immune modulators than small molecule drugs.
status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly requested in point 4 that 'The authors should comment on whether/how their modeling studies apply to the recent reports of long-term responses (cures?) with single agent immunotherapy (CTLA-4, PD1, CD19-CARs).' This direct request indicates the reviewers found the discussion of immunotherapy applicability insufficient and wanted more detailed commentary.

result: The authors quantified tumor burden in 22 patients (7 pancreatic, 11 colorectal, 6 melanoma), finding 1-30 metastatic lesions per patient with total tumor burdens ranging from 9×10^8 to 3×10^11 cells.
status_reasoning: While reviewers did not challenge the data collection itself, point 7 requests that authors 'include both measurements on relevant figures, perhaps in the form of a conversion scale, to make it easier for clinicians to appreciate the clinical relevance.' This suggests the presentation of tumor burden data needed improvement for clinical interpretation, though the data itself was not questioned.

result: The mathematical model derives formulas for expected numbers of resistant cells: X ≈ M n12 μ when cross-resistance mutations exist (n12 ≥ 1), and X ≈ M n1n2 μ² without cross-resistance (n12 = 0). This shows tumor cells are more likely to become resistant through one cross-resistance mutation than through sequential mutations.
status_reasoning: Reviewers praised the work as 'elegant modeling' and did not challenge the mathematical derivations. While point 8 suggests reconsidering the presentation of mathematical results spread across sections, this is about organization rather than validity. The lack of critique of the mathematical framework indicates acceptance of these theoretical results.

result: Sensitivity analyses show that lesion size and mutation rate are the strongest parameters affecting treatment success. Costly resistance has minimal effect when cross-resistance exists. Combination treatments will be less effective in cancers with increased mutation rates, and even dual therapy without cross-resistance would fail in 37% of patients with high cell turnover.
status_reasoning: Point 5 directly challenges parameter sensitivity by asking 'How would the predictions from the model change if this time [cell doubling] were much different?' This indicates reviewers wanted more thorough sensitivity analysis. The question about cell turnover rate variations suggests uncertainty about how robust the predictions are to parameter changes.

result: The authors conclude that developing drugs acting through distinct pathways with very different chemical structures will be essential for successful combination therapies to circumvent cross-resistance mechanisms.
status_reasoning: Reviewers did not challenge these clinical implications and recommendations. The overall favorable evaluation ('important contribution') and lack of specific critique of these conclusions suggests acceptance of the therapeutic recommendations derived from the modeling work.
